slides.title: Libraries can be bootstrapped: an 8B wrote MRCR's library.
slides.notes: The chain now runs without hand-written code for a new family: proposer writes, verification accepts, a 0.6B caller trained on other families calls it. Stress the caveat: MRCR is a parsing task in disguise, so this is program discovery. The ladder: the 8B and a 4-bit 14B, both thinking, each succeed on 2 of 5 seeds; scale does not make discovery reliable, though the 14B succeeds sooner when it does. Every trained 4B fails.

slides.title: Discovery on 37 generated families: thinking, scale, and training.
slides.notes: Generated families give resolution MRCR cannot: 37 held-out families per proposer. Thinking and scale both matter. Training the 4B works: SFT on the 8B's verified code transfers parsing to new string formats, and 40 steps of RL with the verified teaching score as reward lift held-out discovery from 9 to 30 of 74 attempts (p < 0.001), close to the 8B on string formats. Round four, with more varied helper-family teacher data, reaches 42 of 74, statistically level with the 8B (45) and 14B (47) at a twentieth of the tokens. The remaining gap was helper use. With three times the helper-family teacher data (from the 8B and 14B, worked example stripped), the 4B reaches the 8B's mean score on helper families, giving up about six code families (not significant). Two RL seeds of the same recipe differed by four families, so RL recipe comparisons need several seeds. Verification: with all candidates drawn, a candidate that runs cleanly on the teaching inputs and reproduces the three worked examples in its prompt is almost always correct (precision 0.81, 0.88, 0.98 with one, two, three labels), so on program-solvable families the label cost is about three examples; agreement among candidates fails because a trained proposer repeats its mistakes. It does not reach MRCR.

slides.title: Bootstrapping is cheap where answers are exact (pre-registered).
slides.notes: The day's main result, tested prospectively and replicated with a second bootstrap seed (pooled 26 against 29 of 60, one false acceptance in 60). On 30 families neither proposer had seen, a 4B trained on the 8B's verified libraries, sampling eight candidates and accepting by the three worked examples in its own prompt, bootstraps as many correct libraries as the thinking 8B with the full protocol and thirty labels, at a fourteenth of the tokens and with no false acceptances. The mechanism is the label curve: on exact families a program that reproduces three examples and runs cleanly on the other inputs is almost always right. The limit matters: on noisy families (MuSiQue F1, OOLONG classification) a few labels cannot rank close candidates.

slides.title: One line of documentation decides whether an untrained caller uses a library.
slides.notes: The cleanest result of the day. Same code, four docstrings. The usage line alone carries the effect. The practical rule: every library ships with a usage line; the bootstrapper now inserts one. The deeper point: an untrained caller reads documentation, a distilled caller has learned the call.

slides.title: MuSiQue in long haystacks: capacity belongs in choosing evidence.
slides.notes: MuSiQue is where the routine needs helper calls. The two-round library wins on accuracy and cost through the 0.6B caller. Everything that adds capacity elsewhere (recursion, bigger reader, more samples) does not help. The gap to gold paragraphs (about 0.2) is evidence selection.

slides.title: External validity, and what we withdrew.
slides.notes: LongBench-v2 is the external-validity check. The first generic library (map-reduce notes) tied direct reading at nine times the cost; a retrieval library (BM25 over passages for the question and each option, one read) beats direct reading on all 503 questions, 0.427 against 0.356 (+0.07, se 0.02), at a quarter of its tokens, also through the 0.6B caller; the first 150-question sample had suggested +0.11. The lesson matches MuSiQue: choose evidence, do not summarize everything. Two earlier readings were withdrawn after fresh samples. The method lessons are the ones that cost most: scripted harnesses that did not match the kernel, verification sets that did not span deployment lengths.
